title: Differential Leukocyte Count

references.label: Standard clinical hematology laboratory textbooks/manuals (e.g. Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management)
CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

purpose: To classify and enumerate the proportion of each white blood cell type (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils, and any abnormal cells) on a stained peripheral blood smear.
principle: White blood cell types differ in nuclear shape, chromatin pattern, and cytoplasmic granularity when stained with a Romanowsky-type stain, allowing a trained examiner (or an automated analyzer using similar morphologic/light-scatter cues) to classify each cell counted in a systematic scan of the smear's monolayer region.
requiredMaterials: Manual differential counter (tally device), if performed manually

procedure.instruction: Scan the smear at low power to select a well-distributed monolayer region (avoiding the very thick body and the extreme feathered edge).
Switch to oil immersion (1000×) and systematically scan the selected region using a consistent pattern (e.g. a battlement track) to avoid recounting the same field.

procedure.note: The specific total-cell target is a method convention (100 is widely used) and should follow the laboratory's validated procedure.
procedure.instruction: Classify each white cell encountered by type and tally using a differential counter, continuing until a standard total count is reached (commonly 100 cells, per the laboratory's method).
Note any morphologic abnormalities observed in white cells, red cells, or platelets during the same scan (e.g. toxic granulation, left shift, blasts, red cell shape abnormalities).
Convert tallied counts to percentages, and correlate with the automated analyzer's WBC count and differential (if available) for consistency.

observations: Record the percentage (and, using the total WBC count, the absolute count) of each cell type, plus any morphologic abnormalities noted.
interpretation: A relative increase in one cell type (e.g. neutrophilia) must be interpreted alongside the absolute WBC count, since a normal WBC count can still contain a skewed differential, and vice versa; morphologic findings (e.g. blasts, marked left shift) can be as clinically significant as the percentages themselves.
precautions: Perform on a well-made smear only — a poor smear distorts cell distribution and morphology.
Maintain a consistent, non-overlapping scan pattern to avoid sampling bias.
limitations: Manual differentials carry inherent inter-observer variability; automated analyzer differentials are generally more reproducible for normal-range samples but flag abnormal/atypical populations for manual (smear) review rather than replacing it entirely.
biosafetyNotes: Handle stained slides as biohazardous material; standard precautions apply.
